title: Bamidbar: teachers are parents (Numbers 3:1)
hook: Aaron's sons are called Moses' too; whoever teaches a child is like a parent (Sanhedrin 19b)

segments.voice: Yesterday the Levites were set apart, and your line was set apart to serve. Did a quiet server get thanked, or helped? Day four hundred thirty-four.

Most of us can name one. The teacher who stayed after class. The coach who saw something in a kid nobody else did. The aunt who taught you to read music, the neighbor who taught you to ride a bike, the camp counselor whose voice you still hear when you're scared. They aren't on your birth certificate. But if someone asked who made you who you are, their names would come up fast. The Torah has a verse that seems, at first, to have made a mistake in a family tree. The rabbis decided it hadn't.
screen: `THE ONE WHO STAYED AFTER CLASS.` → `NOT ON THE BIRTH CERTIFICATE.` → `A FAMILY TREE THAT LOOKS WRONG.`

segments.voice: Numbers three, verse one: "Now these are the generations of Aaron and Moses in the day that the LORD spoke with Moses in mount Sinai." The generations of Aaron and Moses. You'd expect two lists of children. Then verse two names the sons, and they're only Aaron's: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. Moses' own sons aren't there. So why is the heading Aaron and Moses? The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, page nineteen b, answers in a sentence that has been quoted ever since. Aaron fathered them; Moses taught them. And so Scripture counts them as his. Whoever teaches Torah to someone else's child, the Talmud says, it is as if they had given birth to that child. The same page has a sister teaching. In the book of Samuel, some children are named as Michal's, though another woman bore them. The Talmud explains: Michal raised them, and whoever raises an orphan in their home is counted by Scripture as the parent. Put the two together and you get a wide, generous idea of family. Parenthood is something you do as well as something you are. In Jewish tradition, the teacher holds a near-sacred place, and the old law codes discuss honoring one's teacher alongside honoring one's parents. Rashi, reading this very verse, says it plainly: Moses taught them Torah, so they're called his offspring. A family tree, on this reading, has more branches than the birth records show.
screen: `AARON AND MOSES: ONE LIST.` · `ONLY AARON'S SONS ARE NAMED.` · `WHOEVER TEACHES A CHILD.` · `WHOEVER RAISES AN ORPHAN.` · then, large: `TEACHERS ARE PARENTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who taught a child you love. Breathe, and think of a child in your life: your own, a niece, a grandchild, a student, a friend's kid, or the child you once were. Who taught that child something that stuck? A teacher, a coach, a babysitter, a tutor, an older cousin. Picture them. Let yourself feel grateful in a specific way: for this lesson, on that day. Then plan the message you could send them. The bell holds the time.
Bamidbar. This week in the wilderness book: still remembered, be strong, the wilderness teaches, count every head, everyone around the center, set apart to serve, and teachers are parents too.
Your line: teachers are parents too. Today, send the thank-you you planned, even if it's years late. Day four hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition gives teachers great honor; the Talmud's teaching that whoever teaches another's child Torah is as if they gave birth to them is often quoted at teacher-appreciation events and at the close of a child's studies.

what it means: only Aaron's sons are named; Moses is counted as their parent because he taught them.
what a scholar hears: Sanhedrin 19b reads the verse this way, and the same page counts Michal as mother of children she raised.
